title: The heavy ball in the ravine
allegory: Momentum is a heavy ball rolling down a narrow ravine: each gradient is a shove, the ball's velocity remembers past shoves, so shoves that keep agreeing (along the valley) pile up while shoves that flip side to side (across it) cancel.
map: the gradient g at this step
the ball's velocity, remembering old shoves
the momentum buffer v, a decaying running sum of past gradients
the momentum coefficient μ, e.g. 0.9: the share of velocity kept each step
the ball moving along its velocity
the update θ ← θ − η·v instead of θ ← θ − η·g
a ravine: steep walls, gentle floor
pathological curvature: steep in one direction, shallow in another
credit: Ball, velocity and friction framing, and the idea that side-to-side wobbles average out, borrowed from Andrew Ng's 'Gradient descent with momentum' (Deep Learning Specialization, Course 2).

chapters.name: The zig-zag
chapters.note: why is it bouncing instead of rolling?

cap.1: Picture a long, narrow ravine. Plain gradient descent points mostly at the nearest wall, so it bounces side to side and only inches towards the bottom.
cap.2: In a narrow valley the gradient is big across it and tiny along it. Plain SGD follows each gradient, so it zig-zags. This is the [0.3] pathological-curvature plot.
cap.3: Under ill-conditioned curvature the gradient is dominated by the steep axes. The learning rate must stay small enough to be stable there, so progress along the shallow axes crawls.

cap.1: Swap the pebble for a heavy ball. Each slope is a shove, but the ball keeps most of its speed. Shoves that agree add up; shoves that flip cancel.
cap.2: Momentum keeps a running velocity: each step, keep most of the old velocity, add the new gradient, and move along the velocity instead of the raw gradient.
cap.3: The classic heavy-ball update: v ← μv + g, θ ← θ − ηv. The step is an exponentially weighted sum of past gradients: a low-pass filter over the gradient sequence.

parts.note: keep most of the old speed

cap.1: Each step: keep a fraction μ of your old speed (say 0.9), add the new slope, then move along that speed. Friction is the part of speed you lose.
cap.2: PyTorch's SGD does b = μ·b + g, then θ -= lr·b. Set μ = 0 and it is plain SGD. That buffer b is the only extra memory momentum needs.
cap.3: Unrolled, v_t = Σₖ μᵏ g_{t−k}. A constant gradient g gives terminal velocity g/(1−μ), 10× at μ = 0.9; a sign-flipping one is damped towards g/(1+μ).

cap.1: A toy ravine: along the valley the shove is small but always the same; across it, big but flipping sides. The along speed builds; the across speed shrinks.
cap.2: μ = 0.9, along-gradient 0.2 every step, across ±1 alternating. Along velocity climbs towards 2.0; across settles near 0.53. The zig-zag turns into a roll.
cap.3: Consistent components are amplified by up to 1/(1−μ) = 10; alternating ones are attenuated to 1/(1+μ) ≈ 0.53. Momentum reweights directions without ever measuring curvature.

chapters.name: Too little friction
chapters.verdict: Raising μ raises your step size. Retune lr with it.

cap.1: A heavier ball is not always better. With too little friction it flies past the bottom, swings back, and flies past again.
cap.2: Speed builds to about gradient/(1−μ): 10× at μ = 0.9, 100× at 0.99. Bumping μ secretly multiplies your step size, so retune the learning rate with it.
cap.3: Effective step ≈ η/(1−μ) on consistent directions; near μ = 1 the dynamics are underdamped and ring around the minimum. Adam's m averages with (1−β₁), so it has no such terminal-velocity blow-up.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: In code: SGD(momentum=0.9), or just Adam
Adam's first moment is this velocity
Any decaying running average is this rule

cap.1: Momentum is why training rolls instead of rattles. Adam, the optimiser behind the transformers you will open up and steer, carries this same memory.
cap.2: In code it is one argument, SGD(momentum=0.9), and Adam's first moment is the same idea. Any running average that decays then adds, like BatchNorm's running stats, is this rule.
cap.3: Adam = a momentum-style first moment divided by an RMS of gradients, and AdamW trains every transformer later in the course. Its dynamics shape the models you will interpret and steer.

caption.1: Start at μ = 0: plain descent flips wall to wall and inches along. Slide μ to 0.9: it goes about 8× further. Push μ to 0.99 and the sway never settles.
caption.2: Same lr, μ = 0.9 travels about 8× further along the valley, and above lr = 1 plain SGD explodes while momentum stays stable. The price: a slower sway that takes longer to die.
caption.3: Across: heavy ball on Ky²/2 with K = 2, stable for ηK < 2(1+μ), sway shrinking like √μ per step when underdamped. Along: a constant slope amplified towards 1/(1−μ).

where_else: Adam and AdamW: the first moment is a momentum-style running average of gradients
BatchNorm's running mean and variance: decay the old, add the new (PyTorch even names the knob momentum)
Any noisy signal you smooth with an exponential moving average, from loss curves to metrics

hamming.what: Step along a decaying running sum of past gradients instead of the latest gradient alone.
hamming.when: Whenever the loss surface is a narrow valley or the gradients are noisy, which is nearly always; in practice it arrives built into Adam.
hamming.why: Directions that agree step after step get amplified and directions that flip get damped, so the optimiser rolls along the valley instead of rattling across it.

object.title: The velocity ledger
object.subtitle: Ten steps of a ball in a ravine: its speed across the valley (front row) and along it (back row).

cap.1: Two rows of stacks: the ball's speed across the valley (front) and along it (back), step by step. No momentum yet: each speed is just that step's shove.
cap.2: μ = 0 is plain SGD: velocity = gradient. Across: 1 every step, flipping sides. Along: 0.2 every step.
cap.3: Bars show |v_t| per component for a fixed gradient sequence: across alternates ±1, along is a constant 0.2.

cap.1: Give the ball some memory. The along stacks grow as agreeing shoves pile up; the across stacks start to shrink.
cap.2: μ = 0.5: along climbs to 0.4 (2× the shove); across settles near 0.67.
cap.3: Consistent components converge to g/(1−μ); alternating ones to g/(1+μ). The gain depends on how fast the gradient flips.

cap.1: A heavy ball. The along stacks tower over the across stacks now: the ball is rolling down the valley, not bouncing between walls.
cap.2: μ = 0.9: along reaches 1.3 by step 10 and keeps climbing towards 2.0 (10× the shove); across hovers around 0.5.
cap.3: Gain 1/(1−μ) = 10 at zero frequency versus 1/(1+μ) ≈ 0.53 for a gradient flipping every step: a low-pass filter on gradients.

cap.1: Less friction still. Along keeps building, and the across stacks swing high and low for longer. Too heavy and the ball overshoots.
cap.2: μ = 0.95: terminal along speed would be 20× the shove. Speeds this big overshoot the minimum unless the learning rate comes down.
cap.3: As μ → 1 the effective step η/(1−μ) grows without bound and the transient (−μ)ᵗ decays slowly; retune η whenever you raise μ.

cap.1: Adam carries this same memory as its first moment, then divides by a running size of the shoves.
cap.2: Adam's m is a momentum-style average scaled by (1−β₁), so it averages rather than sums; Adam then divides by √v.
cap.3: Adam's m_t = β₁m + (1−β₁)g has unit gain at zero frequency, so there is no terminal-velocity blow-up; the step is m̂/(√v̂ + ε).

predict.q: Along the valley the gradient points the same way every step. With μ = 0.9, how big does the velocity get?

options.t: About the same as one gradient

predict.why: Agreeing shoves pile up: a constant gradient g drives the velocity towards g/(1−μ) = 10g.

predict.q: Across the valley the gradient flips sign every step. What does momentum do to that part?

options.t: Shrinks it: the flips partly cancel

predict.why: Alternating shoves cancel in the running sum, so the across speed settles near g/(1+μ), about half.

predict.q: You raise μ from 0.9 to 0.99 and keep the learning rate. What happens?

options.t: Steps get about 10× bigger and the ball overshoots
Training becomes more careful and stable

predict.why: Terminal speed goes from 10× to 100× the gradient. Raising μ is secretly raising the step size.
